title: Building Reliable Support Agents Using the Effect Typescript Library - Michael Fester

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 26%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is agent architecture: planners that orchestrate actions, workflows, and sub-agents via a custom DSL on Effect. 14.ai is a customer support platform, and Effect serves as the developer platform underlying the entire stack. The talk covers architecture decisions, production deployment, and operational reliability lessons. Prerequisites include TypeScript familiarity and general knowledge of LLM-based systems and agent architectures. The speaker presents a real-world case study of building production support agents with Effect, including architecture and lessons learned. All classification claims are directly stated in the transcript with grade 'said_in_transcript'.

summary: Michael introduces 14.ai, an AI-native customer support platform whose systems interact directly with end users and depend on LLMs in production. He explains that TypeScript alone falls short when handling unreliable APIs, complex dependencies, non-deterministic model outputs, and long-running workflows, and that Effect fills these gaps with type safety, composition primitives, concurrency, interruption and retry, structured error modeling, dependency injection, and OpenTelemetry-based observability. The architecture spans a React frontend, an internal Effect RPC server with a modified TanStack Query, a public Effect HTTP server with autogenerated OpenAPI docs, a data processing engine syncing CRM, docs, and databases, agent workflows written in a custom DSL on Effect, and PostgreSQL for both data and vector storage using Effect SQL. Everything is modeled with Effect schemas, giving runtime validation, encoding/decoding, type-safe I/O, and autogenerated docs. Agents are planners that choose actions, workflows, or sub-agents and repeat until the task is complete. Actions are small focused tool-call-like units; workflows are deterministic multi-step processes; sub-agents group related actions and workflows into domain modules. The custom DSL leverages Effect's functional pipe system to express branching, sequencing, retries, state transitions, and memory. For reliability, the system falls back between LLM providers with similar performance (e.g., GPT-4 mini to Gemini Flash 2.0 for tool calling), using retry policies that track state to avoid retrying failed providers. Token streams are duplicated for user delivery and analytics storage. Testing relies on dependency injection to mock providers and simulate failures. Developer experience strengths include schema-centric design, compile-time DI guarantees, modular composable services, and guard rails that help new engineers avoid bad patterns. Lessons learned emphasize that Effect requires discipline: the clean happy path can create false safety, DI tracing is hard at scale, and the learning curve is real but compounds in value. Michael recommends incremental adoption starting with a single service or endpoint, especially for LLM and AI systems where reliability and observability matter.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Effect extends TypeScript with type safety, structured errors, concurrency, retries, dependency injection, and observability for robust systems.
14.ai uses Effect across the entire stack: React frontend, Effect RPC internal server, Effect HTTP public API, data processing engine, and PostgreSQL via Effect SQL.
Effect schemas provide runtime validation, encoding/decoding, type-safe I/O, and autogenerated documentation across the stack.

Dependency injection enables mocking LLM providers and simulating failure scenarios for testing without touching system internals.
Effect's developer experience benefits include schema-centric design, compile-time DI guarantees, composable services, and guard rails that prevent common mistakes.

sections.title: Introduction and motivation for Effect
sections.summary: Michael introduces 14.ai and explains why Effect is used to handle unreliable APIs, complex dependencies, non-deterministic LLM outputs, and long-running workflows that plain TypeScript cannot manage well.

sections.title: Stack architecture
sections.summary: Describes the full architecture: React frontend, Effect RPC internal server with modified TanStack Query, Effect HTTP public API with autogenerated OpenAPI, data processing engine, custom DSL agent workflows, and PostgreSQL via Effect SQL, all modeled with Effect schemas.

sections.title: Agent model: planners, actions, workflows, sub-agents
sections.summary: Agents are planners that choose actions, workflows, or sub-agents and repeat until completion. Actions are small tool-call-like units, workflows are deterministic multi-step processes, and sub-agents group related capabilities into domain modules, expressed via a custom DSL on Effect's functional pipe system.

sections.title: Reliability and testing
sections.summary: Covers LLM provider fallback with stateful retry policies, duplicated token streams for user delivery and analytics storage, and dependency injection for mocking providers and simulating failures in tests.

sections.title: Developer experience
sections.summary: Highlights schema-centric design with upfront input/output/error types, compile-time DI guarantees, modular composable services, and guard rails that help new TypeScript engineers become productive quickly.

sections.title: Lessons learned and adoption advice
sections.summary: Effect requires discipline: happy-path clarity can hide lost failures, DI is hard to trace at scale, and the learning curve is real but compounds. Michael recommends incremental adoption, especially for LLM/AI systems needing reliability and observability.

limitations: Clean happy-path code can create a false sense of safety and silently lose important failures.
Dependency injection can be hard to trace at scale across multiple layers and subsystems.
Effect has a real learning curve due to its large ecosystem of concepts and tools.
quantitativeClaims: GPT-4 mini can fall back to Gemini Flash 2.0 for tool calling
